crt-tv: The TV. CRT television, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Picture fuzzy? One firm pat on the side really did fix a loose wire sometimes. Two pats is just being mean to the TV. How it works: A beam inside paints the picture one line at a time, super fast. The Real Story: Back then, TVs were big glass boxes with a tube inside that shot tiny beams at the screen to make the picture. That's why they were so deep, so heavy, and why the screen zapped your arm hair. Flat TVs replaced them in the 2000s. Weight: A big one weighed as much as a kid. Back In The Day: Saturday morning cartoons were the main event. Kids got up before their parents, poured a bowl of cereal and sat way too close to the screen. Friday nights were TGIF on ABC, and the whole family watched the same show at the same time, because there was no other way to see it. V-chip: From 2000, new TVs had to let parents block shows. Word On The Playground: It took two grown-ups and one pulled muscle to get it up on the dresser. Rabbit ears wrapped in tinfoil, angled toward wherever the signal felt like being that day. Turning it off left a little white dot that took forever to die. The static zap: The tube runs on so much power the glass holds a charge.
crt-vcr: The VCR. VCR, 1980s, 90s. Childhood Pro Tip: Taping a show? Start the timer five minutes early and stop it five late. The TV clock and the VCR clock never agreed. VHS introduced: 1976, by JVC. The Real Story: The VCR played and recorded VHS tapes. JVC made VHS in 1976, and it beat Sony's Betamax to become the tape everyone used. By the 90s one sat under almost every TV, blinking 12:00. The last ones were made in 2016. Rival format: Sony Betamax, 1975. Back In The Day: If you missed a show, it was gone until the rerun. So somebody in every family learned the VCR timer: channel, start time, stop time, then press Timer and walk away. Get one step wrong and you came home to forty minutes of the weather instead of Goosebumps. A T-120 tape holds: 2 hours at SP, about 6 hours at EP/SLP. Word On The Playground: Eats tapes for fun. Knew a pencil-in-the-reel rescue by age eight. The tracking button was basically a slot machine. Fast-forward made the whole thing whine like it was in pain. Last VCRs made: 2016 (Funai) Why 12:00 blinks: The clock resets whenever the power cuts out.
crt-cable: The cable box. Cable box, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Cable box frozen? Unplug it, count to ten, plug it back in. It really works. You are now a cable technician. Channel guide ran on: Old Commodore Amiga computers. The Real Story: The cable box gave your TV dozens of extra channels and unlocked the ones your family paid for. The scrolling channel guide was the Prevue Channel, which ran on old Amiga computers. In 1999 it became the TV Guide Channel. Became: The TV Guide Channel, in 1999. Back In The Day: Getting cable was a big deal. It meant Nickelodeon, MTV and, from 1992, Cartoon Network, right at home. Kids without it went over to a friend's house to watch Rugrats. The remote was always lost in the couch, so the buttons on the box did most of the work. Fuzzy channels: Paid channels were scrambled unless your family paid. Word On The Playground: The scrambled channels were the forbidden zone. You squinted anyway. Waiting for the guide to scroll back around to your channel. It never came back in time. Green numbers glowing in the dark all night like a tiny nightlight.
nes: Nintendo Entertainment System. Home console, 1985, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: No save button? Write the password on paper the second it shows up. Lose that paper and you start over. US launch: October 18, 1985, in New York first. The Real Story: The Nintendo Entertainment System came out in the US in 1985, made to look like a VCR so stores would sell it. With Super Mario Bros., it brought video games back. Blowing in the cartridge never really fixed it. Pushing it back in did. In Japan it was: The Famicom, from 1983. Back In The Day: Step one: blow on the cartridge. Step two: push it down, hit Power, pray. Every kid in every house did it, every time. Then you played Super Mario Bros. until somebody's mom called up the stairs that it was time to go home. Sold: About 62 million. Word On The Playground: The controller cord was exactly three feet too short. Duck Hunt dog laughed at you and you never forgave him. If somebody hit Reset during a save, a friendship ended. The blinking screen: Worn-out pins in the slot, not dust.
boombox: The boombox. Boombox, 1980s. Childhood Pro Tip: Taping a song off the radio? Finger on Pause, other finger on Record, and let go the second the DJ stops talking. Peak era: Late 1970s to early 1990s. The Real Story: A boombox was a big radio with tape decks and speakers you could carry anywhere. Two tape decks meant you could copy tapes and make mixtapes. They ate a lot of batteries, sometimes ten big D batteries at once. Power: Typically 6 to 10 D batteries, or a wall plug. Back In The Day: On weekends Casey Kasem counted down the American Top 40, and kids sat by the radio with a blank tape ready for their favorite song. Then the boombox went to the park, the pool and the driveway, playing the same tape until it wore thin. Dual decks: Made tape-to-tape dubbing easy at home. Word On The Playground: Every song you taped has the DJ talking over the first ten seconds. The handle is not designed for shoulders. We used it on shoulders. Cassette format: Compact Cassette, introduced by Philips in 1963.
gameboy: Game Boy. Handheld console, 1989, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Trading Pokémon? Plug in the link cable before turning both Game Boys on, and nobody touch the cord till it's done. Came out: July 31, 1989, for $89.95. The Real Story: The Game Boy came out in 1989 with Tetris in the box. Nintendo gave it a simple green screen instead of color so four AA batteries would last for hours. With the Game Boy Color, it sold about 118 million. In the box: Tetris. Back In The Day: The Game Boy made long car rides a lot shorter. It came along to Grandma's, to the dentist's waiting room and under the covers with a clip-on worm light so nobody saw. When the screen started to fade, the batteries were dying and you had about ten minutes left. Screen: Four shades of green-gray. Word On The Playground: You had to tilt it toward a lamp to see anything. Link cable battles in the backseat. It survived a fall down the stairs. The stairs had a dent. Sold: About 118 million, with the Game Boy Color.
tamagotchi: Tamagotchi. Virtual pet, 1997, Bandai. Childhood Pro Tip: Pet beeping during class? Ask to use the bathroom, stay twenty minutes, and clean up its poop in peace. Released: November 23, 1996 (Japan); May 1, 1997 (US) The Real Story: Tamagotchi was a tiny egg-shaped pet on a keychain. You fed it, cleaned up after it, and if you forgot, it died. It came to the US in 1997 and got banned at a lot of schools. About 98 million have been sold. Creators: Aki Maita and Akihiro Yokoi. Back In The Day: In 1997 they sold out everywhere, and kids clipped them to backpacks, belt loops and zipper pulls. Teachers had a whole drawer of them by lunch. When one died, the kid next to you helped hold a little funeral at recess, then you started a new one. Name: Mix of the Japanese 'tamago' (egg) and 'watch' Word On The Playground: Hide it in your sock drawer and it beeps right when Mom opens the drawer. Pulling the battery tab was the closest thing to opening a present. Somebody always says theirs grew up into the "good one". Sold: About 98.1 million (Bandai Namco, 2025)
bed: The bed. Furniture, Never been made. Childhood Pro Tip: Building a fort? Tuck one edge of the blanket under the mattress and hold the other down with big books. Standard twin size: About 38 by 75 inches. The Real Story: The bed was home base for sleepovers, pillow forts and reading with a flashlight after lights out. Twin beds became the normal kid bed in America. Jumping on the bed was banned in every house, and done in every house. Best uses: Fort foundation, trampoline, under-bed storage. Back In The Day: Sleepovers meant sleeping bags all over the floor, a rented movie, a pizza, and whispering way past midnight until somebody's dad said "Go to sleep" for the third time. This bed has hosted every one of them, plus one "it was the dog" situation that is still not discussed. Under-bed storage: Usually socks, snacks and one missing library book. Word On The Playground: Monsters live under it. Snacks live under it too, so it evens out. Making it every morning was a rule that lasted three days. The quilt has been washed so many times the pattern gave up.
bed-pillow: The smiley pillow. Fair prize, Prize from the fair. Childhood Pro Tip: Pillow fight rule: hit with the smiley side first. Nobody can stay mad at a face that happy. Smiley designed: 1963, by Harvey Ball. The Real Story: The smiley face was drawn in 1963 by an artist named Harvey Ball. He got paid $45 for it and never owned the rights. It ended up on buttons, shirts and carnival prizes everywhere. Original client: State Mutual Life Assurance Company. Back In The Day: Won at the county fair for three tickets after missing the ring toss eleven times. The fair was the best week of summer: corn dogs, the Gravitron, and a game booth that never really let you win. It has absorbed tears, drool and one whole juice box. Still smiling. Ball's fee: $45. Word On The Playground: Smells faintly of Kool-Aid forever. Flip it over at night so it isn't smiling at you in the dark. Trademark: Ball never registered one.
backpack: The backpack. School bag, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Write your name on the inside tag in marker on day one. Half the class had the same JanSport. JanSport founded: 1967, Seattle. The Real Story: Backpacks became normal school gear in the 70s and 80s, with brands like JanSport. By the 90s your backpack showed who you were: pins, patches, keychains and your name in marker. One strap or two was a real debate. Common material: Nylon or Cordura fabric. Back In The Day: Back to school started at the store, picking out a Trapper Keeper, Lisa Frank folders and a new backpack. By June, the bottom held a permission slip from October, a flattened Lunchable, three pencils with no erasers and a library book that is now officially stolen. Decor of choice: Pins, patches, keychains and markered names. Word On The Playground: Worn on one shoulder for six years. Looking cool cost a lot of back pain. The zipper broke in October. It stayed broken until June.
beanbag: The bean bag. Furniture, 1968. Childhood Pro Tip: Shake it up before you sit. Grab both sides and fluff it, or you'll end up sitting on the floor in a sack. Original design: Sacco, 1968. The Real Story: The bean bag chair started as a fancy Italian chair in 1968, a bag full of tiny foam beads that shapes itself around you. Cheaper ones landed in kids' rooms everywhere. Getting out of one gracefully is still impossible. Designers: Piero Gatti, Cesare Paolini, Franco Teodoro. Back In The Day: Lots of 90s kids' rooms had one, usually in a loud color or with a team logo. It was the best seat for video games because you could sink in right in front of the TV. One seam always leaked foam beads, and they turned up in the carpet for years. Maker: Zanotta (Italy) Word On The Playground: Everybody fought over it during sleepovers. Getting out of it took two tries and a noise. Filling: Expanded polystyrene beads.
window: The window. Window, Grounded view. Childhood Pro Tip: Hear the ice cream truck? You have about one song to grab couch change, find your shoes and get to the curb. Go now. Mini blind slats: Usually about 1 inch wide. The Real Story: Thin mini blinds were in almost every 80s and 90s house. Summer nights meant a box fan in the window and loud bugs outside. Some cicadas only come out every 13 or 17 years, so some summers were way louder. Periodical cicadas: Come up on 13- or 17-year cycles. Back In The Day: Summer break meant playing outside until the streetlights came on. That was the rule in a lot of houses. Kids rode bikes, played tag and knocked on doors to see who could come out. If you were grounded, you watched it all from here through one bent blind slat. Can-and-string phone: Works only if the string is pulled tight. Word On The Playground: Opening the window at night meant one more bug in the room. Worth it.
window-south: The back window. Window, Streetlight side. Childhood Pro Tip: Can't sleep? Count the headlights sliding across the ceiling. Nobody ever made it past twenty. Streetlight type: Orange power-saving lamps. The Real Story: That orange glow outside came from streetlights made to save power. Their orange light made every color look the same at night. Most towns have since switched to bright white LED lights. Replaced by: White LED streetlights. Back In The Day: At night the streetlight out back turned the whole room orange, and the tree outside threw moving shadows on the wall. Before phones, falling asleep meant lying in the dark with your thoughts and the sound of the house settling. Word On The Playground: Rain on this window was the best sleep sound ever made.
door: The door. Door, KEEP OUT (this means you) Childhood Pro Tip: Door won't stay shut? Fold a piece of paper a few times and wedge it by the latch. It stays closed, no lock needed. Lock type: Privacy lockset, push-button or turn-button. The Real Story: Bedroom door locks aren't real locks. There's a little hole on the outside so anyone can pop it open with a thin tool in an emergency. That's how every parent got in. KEEP OUT signs were mostly for show. Emergency release: A small hole or slot on the outside knob. Back In The Day: Slamming the door was how arguments ended in the 90s. Every "You're not the boss of me!" ended right here, followed by "Don't slam that door!" from downstairs. The KEEP OUT sign went up the same week. Real effectiveness: Low. Parents always got in. Word On The Playground: Knock first. Nobody knocked first. Every parent knew the trick to open it. Every kid pretended they didn't.
door-poster: "I Want to Believe" poster. Poster, 1993. Childhood Pro Tip: Watching The X-Files? Sit with your back to the wall so nothing sneaks up behind you. It doesn't help. Premiered: September 10, 1993, on Fox. The Real Story: The X-Files started on TV in 1993. Two FBI agents, Mulder and Scully, chased aliens and weird mysteries. Mulder had an 'I Want to Believe' poster with a UFO in his office, and kids everywhere hung one too. Created by: Chris Carter. Back In The Day: The X-Files was on Friday nights at first, then moved to Sundays, and the next day the whole school talked about the scary episode. We were too scared to watch the whole thing, but we still wanted the poster. Mom thought it was about Jesus. Stars: David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson. Word On The Playground: Stayed up for the theme song and then hid under the blanket for the rest. Whistling the theme song in a dark hallway was a whole move. Original run: 9 seasons, 1993, 2002. Tagline: The truth is out there.
door-cap: Space Invaders cap. Arcade prize, 1978, Taito. Childhood Pro Tip: Skee-Ball trick: roll it soft and straight up the middle. The 40 hole lands way more than the 100s. Released: 1978 (Japan) The Real Story: Space Invaders came out in 1978 and was one of the first giant video game hits. Rows of aliens march down at you. They speed up as you shoot them because the machine has fewer to draw. That was an accident, and it made the game better. Designer: Tomohiro Nishikado. Back In The Day: The arcade at the mall was the place to be on a Saturday. Quarters went into Street Fighter II, tickets came out of Skee-Ball, and 4,000 of them got you this cap from the prize counter. It hangs on the door because hats indoors were "disrespectful". Publisher: Taito; Midway in the US. Word On The Playground: Worn backwards, obviously. Never washed. Will never be washed. Speed-up: The aliens move faster as fewer remain on screen.
door-pins: The pin collection. Pins, Planet, smiley, alien, star. Childhood Pro Tip: Lost the back of a pin? Push a pencil eraser onto the point. It holds better than the real one. Celluloid button patent: 1896, Whitehead and Hoag. The Real Story: People have collected and traded pins for more than 100 years. In the 90s they went on jean jackets, hats and backpacks. Pin trading is still a big hobby, especially at theme parks. Common types: Pin-back buttons and enamel lapel pins. Back In The Day: Every pin here was a trade. The alien cost two Pokémon cards and a pudding cup. The star came free in a cereal box. In the 90s you could tell who someone was from across the hall just by their pins. Best display: The backpack, until it rips. Word On The Playground: Every pin poked your finger at least once. Pinned to the backpack until the backpack ripped.
nightstand: The nightstand. Furniture, Mission control. Childhood Pro Tip: Keep a flashlight in the drawer. Storms knock the power out, and the family flashlight always has dead batteries. Usual contents: Alarm clock, lamp, contraband candy. The Real Story: The bedside table was mission control: alarm clock, lamp, and a drawer full of things that weren't supposed to be there. Most were cheap wood-look boards, and the drawer stuck unless you lifted it as you pulled. Drawer trick: Lift and pull. Back In The Day: Everything important lived within arm's reach of the pillow: the alarm clock, a cup of water and, if you could sneak it upstairs, the cordless phone. Late-night calls under the covers with your best friend were the whole point of a cordless phone. Typical material: Particleboard with a wood-look finish. Word On The Playground: Candy goes in the back of the drawer, behind the socks, under the Game Boy instructions. The drawer sticks unless you lift and pull. Learned that by age five.
ns-clock: Alarm clock. Clock radio, 1990s, RCA. Childhood Pro Tip: Put the alarm clock across the room. You have to get out of bed to turn it off, and by then you're up. Display: Red seven-segment LED. The Real Story: Red number clock radios sat on every nightstand. Big glowing numbers, a radio, an alarm, and a snooze button as big as the top. When the power blinked, they lost the time, so half the clocks in America flashed 12:00. Snooze buttons: Introduced on alarm clocks in the 1950s. Back In The Day: Before cell phones, this was how you woke up for school: red numbers, a loud beep, and a snooze button big enough to hit with your eyes closed. On weekends you stayed up just to watch it flip to 12:00 and felt like a rebel. Classic snooze length: About 9 minutes on many models. Word On The Playground: Red numbers you could see from space. Set it seven minutes fast so you'd be early. Hit snooze seven times. Late anyway. After a power cut: Blinks 12:00 until someone sets it.
ns-lava: Lava lamp. Lava lamp, 1963. Childhood Pro Tip: Do not shake the lava lamp. If you shake the lava lamp, do not tell anyone you shook the lava lamp. Invented: 1963, by Edward Craven Walker. The Real Story: A British man named Edward Craven Walker invented the lava lamp in 1963 after seeing a homemade egg timer bubbling in a pub. A bulb warms a blob of wax so it rises, cools and sinks. They came back big in the 90s. First model: The Astro. Back In The Day: Every mall in the 90s had a gift shop with a whole wall of lava lamps glowing in the dark, and that's where most of them came from. On the nightstand it doubled as a nightlight, a slow, blobby one. How it works: Heated wax becomes less dense, rises, cools and sinks. Word On The Playground: Swearing you saw a blob shaped exactly like a dinosaur. Too hot to touch, so naturally everybody touched it. Why shaking ruins it: It mixes wax into the liquid and turns it cloudy.
ns-mug: Smiley mug. Mug, Hot cocoa only. Childhood Pro Tip: Hot cocoa trick: stir in a splash of cold milk. It's cool enough to drink before the marshmallows melt. Recipe: One packet, hot water or milk, stir. The Real Story: Instant hot cocoa packets were made for snow days and after school, with tiny dried marshmallows right in the mix. A mug you made in art class was the official cup. A hard old marshmallow at the bottom was tradition. Marshmallows: Tiny dehydrated ones, already in the mix. Back In The Day: Snow days were the best days. You spent the morning sledding and came inside soaked to the bone, with red cheeks and wet socks. Hot cocoa in this mug, made for Mother's Day in art class and then quietly taken back, was how every snow day ended. Best served: Snow days and after sledding. Word On The Playground: Art class glaze, a little lumpy, still holds cocoa just fine. Correct marshmallow count: too many.
ns-teddy: Night-shift bear. Teddy bear, 1902. Childhood Pro Tip: Monsters can't get you if a bear is watching the closet. Sit him facing the closet, not the bed. Known rule. Named after: President Theodore Roosevelt. The Real Story: The teddy bear is named after President Teddy Roosevelt. In 1902 he refused to shoot a tied-up bear on a hunting trip, a newspaper drew a cartoon of it, and a shop owner started selling stuffed 'Teddy's bears.' Origin story: A 1902 hunting trip in Mississippi. Back In The Day: Almost every kid had a bear on night watch. Lights out, closet door shut all the way, and one bear on guard. This one has never let a single monster through. Perfect record. Early makers: Morris Michtom (US) and Steiff (Germany) Word On The Playground: Lost an eye in a tug-of-war. Still on duty. Inspired by: A Clifford Berryman newspaper cartoon.
ns-recorder: The blue Sony. Tape recorder, 1980s, Sony. Childhood Pro Tip: Press Record and Play down together. On a lot of tape recorders, Record alone won't go. Cassette format: Compact Cassette, Philips, 1963. The Real Story: Cassette tapes came out in 1963, and small tape recorders let anyone record their voice, the radio or music. Sony even made bright My First Sony recorders for kids. Hearing your own voice played back was a shock. Kids' line: My First Sony, late 1980s. Back In The Day: Before anybody had a camera in their pocket, a tape recorder was how you made a show. Kids recorded fake radio shows with their cousins, songs off the radio and the family singing Happy Birthday. Somewhere in a shoebox there's a forty-minute tape that should never be played. Classic trick: Hold Pause, wait for the song, release. Word On The Playground: Prank calls were recorded. Allegedly. Every recording starts with somebody whispering "Is it on?"
ns-yoshi: Yoshi sticker. Sticker, 1990, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Fastest way to the cereal-box prize: pour the whole box into a mixing bowl. Act natural. Debut: Super Mario World (1990) The Real Story: Yoshi first showed up in Super Mario World, which came with the Super Nintendo in 1991. He's a green dinosaur who eats bad guys with his long tongue and lets Mario ride on his back. Designer: Shigefumi Hino. Back In The Day: Cereal boxes used to have toys and stickers inside, sealed in a little plastic bag at the bottom. Kids picked the cereal by the prize, not the taste. This sticker took two days of eating a whole box to get, and it went on the drawer the second it came out. Signature move: Eating enemies with his tongue. Word On The Playground: Worth the stomach ache. It's never coming off. We tried. Famous sound: A little 'yoshi!' when you hop on.
ns-tapes: The bedtime stack. Book stack, 1992, 1997. Childhood Pro Tip: Reading after lights out? Put a towel along the bottom of the door so the hallway can't see the flashlight. First book: Welcome to Dead House, July 1992. The Real Story: Goosebumps started in 1992 with Welcome to Dead House. R.L. Stine wrote 62 books in the first series, and at its peak it sold about four million copies a month. Every chapter ended on a scary cliffhanger. Original series: 62 books, 1992, 1997. Back In The Day: The Scholastic book order form came home in your backpack, and you circled half the page. Book order day, when the box came to class, felt like a holiday. Goosebumps covers were the thing everybody wanted, all bright colors and a monster on the front. Author: R.L. Stine. Word On The Playground: "Reader beware" was not a suggestion. When the flashlight died, you just lay there thinking about the Haunted Mask. Cover artist: Tim Jacobus. Tagline: Reader beware, you're in for a scare!
ns-vhs: Movie night tapes. VHS tapes, 1993, 1995. Childhood Pro Tip: Favorite tape going fuzzy? Run a head-cleaning tape through the VCR. It looks blank and works like magic. Jurassic Park: June 11, 1993, directed by Steven Spielberg. The Real Story: Three movie night favorites. Jurassic Park (1993) mixed robot dinosaurs with computer ones. Hocus Pocus (1993) flopped in theaters and became a Halloween classic on tape. Toy Story (1995) was the first movie made all on computers. Hocus Pocus: July 16, 1993, directed by Kenny Ortega. Back In The Day: Movie night meant the same few tapes over and over. Hocus Pocus came out every October, Jurassic Park every Tuesday, and Toy Story whenever a little cousin came over. Watching the same movie fifty times wasn't weird. It was normal. Toy Story: November 22, 1995, Pixar. Word On The Playground: Hocus Pocus is worn thin right at the part where they sing. Jurassic Park has a crinkle in the kitchen scene from being paused too many times. Toy Story first: First fully computer-animated feature film.
ns-gameboy: Backup Game Boy. Handheld console, 1989, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Rechargeable batteries cost more but pay for themselves in about a month. Every Game Boy kid learned this the hard way. Model number: DMG-01. The Real Story: The first Game Boy ran on four AA batteries and was really tough. One got caught in a fire during the 1991 Gulf War and still worked, and Nintendo showed it off in its New York store. Nintendo made Game Boys until 2003. Power: 4 AA batteries. Back In The Day: The spare one, for when the main Game Boy's batteries died at the worst possible moment. In a lot of houses batteries were a big deal, kept in the kitchen drawer and counted. When they ran out, you took them from the TV remote and blamed the cat. Famous survivor: A fire-damaged Game Boy from the Gulf War that still worked. Word On The Playground: Every house had one TV remote with no batteries in it. This is why. Successor: Game Boy Color, 1998.
south-shelf: The high shelf. Shelf, Display only, do not touch. Childhood Pro Tip: High shelf rule: if a little cousin can reach it, it's no longer yours. Stack accordingly. Purpose: Display only. The Real Story: Every 90s kid had a shelf for the most important stuff: collectibles, the good Game Boy, and toys too old to play with but too loved to give away. Up high, away from little cousins. Threat level: Little cousins. Back In The Day: When family came over for the holidays, the good stuff went up here. Little cousins got the toy bins. Big Ted, the lava lamp, the good Game Boy and the View-Master nobody remembers how to load stayed safe, out of reach. Access method: Spinning desk chair (not recommended) Word On The Playground: Needed the desk chair to reach it. The chair spins. That went great.
sh-lava: The other lava lamp. Lava lamp, 1965. Childhood Pro Tip: Lava lamp homework method: check on it every five minutes. Lava done, homework not done. US rights bought: 1965, by Wertheimer and Spector. The Real Story: In 1965 two American businessmen saw the lava lamp at a trade show in Germany and started selling it in the US as the Lava Lite. Lava lamps were huge in the 60s, faded away, then came back big in the 90s. US brand name: Lava Lite. Back In The Day: In the 90s a lava lamp was the go-to present for any kid who was hard to shop for. Every aunt knew it. This one came on a birthday with a card that said "Groovy!" and it sat on the shelf glowing purple for years. Warm-up time: Usually an hour or more to flow well. Word On The Playground: Named it. It never answered. Blobs stuck at the top: Usually means the lamp is running too hot.
sh-vhs: Home Alone, Jurassic Park, Aladdin. VHS tapes, 1990, 1993. Childhood Pro Tip: Home Alone traps work great on burglars. On dads, less great. Test on a pillow first. Home Alone: November 16, 1990. The Real Story: Home Alone (1990) was one of the biggest comedies ever. Aladdin (1992), with Robin Williams as the Genie, was the top movie of its year. Jurassic Park (1993) was the biggest movie ever made, until Titanic. Aladdin: November 1992; Disney's white clamshell VHS. Back In The Day: Disney movies came out on tape in big white plastic cases, and every kid had a stack of them. Home Alone was on every holiday, and every kid tried a trap at least once. Ours was a paint can on a string over the door. It got Dad. Jurassic Park: June 11, 1993. Word On The Playground: Rewound the trap scene until the tape got wobbly. The Aladdin tape is the white clamshell one. The good one. 'Keep the change, ya filthy animal': From Angels with Filthy Souls, a fake gangster movie made for Home Alone.
sh-car: Red Hot Wheels. Die-cast car, 1968, Mattel. Childhood Pro Tip: Want to win the race? Pick your heaviest car. The heavy ones beat the light ones down the orange track. Launched: 1968. The Real Story: Mattel made Hot Wheels in 1968 to beat Matchbox cars. Their wheels barely touched anything, so they flew down the orange track. The very first one made was a dark blue Camaro. Maker: Mattel. Back In The Day: Hot Wheels cost about a dollar each at the grocery store checkout, right where kids could see them. Every trip with Mom was a chance to beg for one more. This red one won every race on the loop, except when it flew off and hit the dog. First line: The 'Sweet Sixteen' Word On The Playground: The orange track connectors left marks on everything. Paint chips from launching it off the stairs. For science. Scale: About 1:64. First car produced: Dark blue Custom Camaro.
sh-teddy: Big Ted. Teddy bear, 1902. Childhood Pro Tip: Being too old for teddy bears ends the moment thunder starts. Nobody needs to know. Steiff founded by: Margarete Steiff. The Real Story: In 1903 a German toy company called Steiff brought its teddy bear to a big toy fair, and an American store ordered thousands. That started the teddy bear craze. Real Steiff bears still have a little button in one ear. Big break: Leipzig Toy Fair, 1903. Back In The Day: Big Ted came to every tea party, sat in the car seat next to you, and rode in the shopping cart to the store. He went through the washing machine four times. Retired to the high shelf around fourth grade, where he can still see the whole room. Trademark: The 'Button in Ear' Word On The Playground: The bow tie has been retied by every person in the family. Classic material: Mohair plush.
sh-gameboy: The good Game Boy. Handheld console, 1989, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Taking the Game Boy to school? Turn the volume all the way down before you leave the house, not in class. US release day sales: About 40,000. The Real Story: Game Boys were the thing teachers took away most in the 90s. In the US, 40,000 sold on day one. Pokémon Red and Blue in 1998 kept it going for years after other game systems from its time were gone. Japanese launch: 300,000 units sold out in two weeks. Back In The Day: Bringing a Game Boy to school was risky. Teachers took them away and gave them back at the end of the day, or sometimes the end of the week. This one spent a terrifying weekend in the principal's desk. It lives up here now. Safe. Late-life hit: Pokémon Red and Blue (US, 1998) Word On The Playground: The principal definitely played it over the weekend. Discontinued: 2003.
sh-turtle: Leonardo. Action figure, 1988, Playmates. Childhood Pro Tip: Playing Ninja Turtles with friends? Call Leonardo first. He's the leader, so you're technically in charge. Created by: Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird, 1984. The Real Story: The Ninja Turtles started as a comic book in 1984. The cartoon came in 1987 and the toys in 1988, and they were some of the best-selling toys of the time. Leonardo wears blue and fights with two swords. Toy line: Playmates Toys, from 1988. Back In The Day: Everybody wanted to be Raphael or Michelangelo, so you got stuck with Leonardo and acted like you didn't care. You cared. The figures came with tiny weapons, and both of his swords were gone by Christmas. Leonardo's mask: Blue. Word On The Playground: "Cowabunga" was a full answer to any question. Turtle-shaped pizza was technically just pizza. Weapon: Two katanas. Named after: Leonardo da Vinci.
sh-viewmaster: View-Master. Toy viewer, 1939. Childhood Pro Tip: Point it at a lamp or a window for brighter pictures. Never point it at the sun. Ask someone who tried. Introduced: Around 1939. The Real Story: The View-Master came out around 1939. Each paper reel holds seven pairs of tiny photos, one for each eye, so the pictures pop out in 3D. It started as a travel souvenir and turned into a classic kids' toy. Original company: Sawyer's (Portland, Oregon) Back In The Day: View-Master reels came in little paper envelopes, with cartoons, movies and faraway places on them. Kids got them at gift shops on family trips, and somehow you looked at the same Grand Canyon reel four hundred times. Inventor: William Gruber. Word On The Playground: The orange lever had the most satisfying click in history. Each reel: 7 stereo scenes (14 tiny images)
sh-books: Goosebumps and The Lost World. Books, 1993, 1995. Childhood Pro Tip: Carry the big book to look smart. Actually read the Goosebumps. Nobody needs the details. The Lost World: 1995, by Michael Crichton. The Real Story: The Lost World (1995) was the sequel to Jurassic Park, and the movie came in 1997. Night of the Living Dummy (1993) was the Goosebumps book that brought us Slappy, the creepy dummy who became the most famous villain in the series. Movie version: 1997, directed by Steven Spielberg. Back In The Day: Reading programs like Book It! gave you a free Pizza Hut pizza for reading books. So kids read a lot, especially short ones. The Lost World was way too long for a fifth grader, but it had a T. rex on the cover. Goosebumps you actually read. Twice. Night of the Living Dummy: Goosebumps #7, 1993. Word On The Playground: Nobody ever finished The Lost World. Not even the teacher. Villain introduced: Slappy the Dummy.
toyshelf: The toy cubby. Toy storage, Where everything got thrown at cleanup time. Childhood Pro Tip: Cleaning your room takes ninety seconds if you don't look at what goes in which bin. Method: Throw it in the bin. The Real Story: Cube shelves with bins became the toy storage every kid's room had. 'Clean your room' meant throw everything in the closest bin. Whatever went in there wasn't seen again for months. Average time: Under 90 seconds. Back In The Day: "Go clean your room" was the most said sentence in the 90s. Archaeologists will one day dig into these bins and find a Pokémon box, three socks and a single roller skate. Contents: A Pokémon box, socks, one roller skate. Word On The Playground: The bins never closed. They were never meant to close.
ts-teddy: Scruffy. Teddy bear, Loved too hard. Childhood Pro Tip: A teddy with no fur on one ear is how you know it's been doing its job. Never let anybody fix that. Psychology term: Transitional object. The Real Story: Most kids had one stuffed animal that went everywhere and came back worn out from being loved. Doctors even have a name for it: a comfort object that helps kids feel safe as they grow up. Described by: Donald Winnicott, 1951. Back In The Day: Scruffy went everywhere: the store, the car, the bath, and the dog's mouth once. If he got left at a restaurant, the whole family drove back. Every 90s family had a story about the stuffed animal they almost lost. Common repair: Mom with a needle and thread. Word On The Playground: Mom sewed his arm back on during a sleepover emergency. All the fur rubbed off one ear from being held while falling asleep.
ts-handheld: Pocket game. LCD handheld, 1990s, Tiger Electronics. Childhood Pro Tip: High scores don't save. Write yours on the back of the box in marker so everybody knows. Company started: 1978. The Real Story: Tiger Electronics made cheap handheld games of everything from Batman to Sonic. Each one played just one game, with pictures already printed on the screen that lit up. Toy maker Hasbro bought Tiger in 1998. Screen: Pictures printed in, they just light up. Back In The Day: Tiger handhelds cost about twenty dollars and were everywhere at Christmas and birthday parties. One game, one sound effect, no pause button. This one came from a birthday party goodie bag and kept everybody busy for a whole car ride. Games per unit: One. Word On The Playground: The beep. Just the beep. Forever. The pictures on the screen never moved, they just lit up. Bought by Hasbro: 1998.
ts-clock: Clock radio. Clock radio, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Set the alarm to radio, not buzzer. Waking up to a stranger talking about traffic is weird, but at least it's somebody. Bands: AM and FM. The Real Story: Clock radios put an alarm and a radio in one box by the bed, so you could wake up to music or the morning DJ instead of a buzzer. The radio wire had to be moved around until the station came in. Wake modes: Buzzer or radio. Back In The Day: On snowy mornings, the whole family listened to this. The radio read the list of school closings in alphabetical order, and you lay there waiting for your school's name. If it came, you went back to sleep happy. FM antenna: Often a thin wire you moved until it worked. Word On The Playground: The radio station only came in if the antenna wire touched the window.
ts-skateboard: The RAD skateboard. Skateboard, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Learning to skate? Find your balance on the grass first, then move to the driveway. It hurts less. Origins: California, 1950s. The Real Story: Skateboarding started with California surfers in the 1950s and took off in 1972 when new rubbery wheels gave boards real grip. In 1999 Tony Hawk landed the first 900, two and a half spins in the air, at the X Games. Urethane wheels: Frank Nasworthy, 1972. Back In The Day: In the 90s, skateboarding was everywhere: Tony Hawk was on TV, skate shops were in every mall, and kids wore skate shoes who had never touched a board. We learned exactly one trick: sitting on it and rolling down the driveway. Still a skater. First 900: Tony Hawk, X Games, 1999. Word On The Playground: The stickers are worth more than the board. The griptape shredded three pairs of jeans and one knee. Griptape: Sandpaper-like sheet on the top of the deck.
ts-vhs: Recorded-off-TV tapes. VHS tapes, 1980s, 90s. Childhood Pro Tip: Label every tape with what's on it and the date. Then tape over it anyway. The label is more of a guess. Key ruling: Sony Corp. v. Universal City Studios, January 1984. The Real Story: Taping shows off TV onto blank VHS tapes was a family hobby, and in 1984 the Supreme Court said it was legal. The slowest speed fit six hours on one tape, but the picture looked worse. Decision: Home 'time-shifting' is fair use. Back In The Day: Families recorded everything: the Super Bowl, a special TV movie, Grandma's favorite show. Tapes got reused over and over, so most of them say one thing on the label and have something else on them. The one marked "Lion King" is a Bills game and twenty minutes of a cooking show. Speeds: SP (best), LP, EP/SLP (longest) Word On The Playground: Commercials included, which, honestly, were the best part. Bonus content: The commercials.
ts-lava: Orange lava lamp. Lava lamp, 1992, Mathmos. Childhood Pro Tip: Lava lamps need the whole outlet. Your Game Boy charger can wait. Priorities. Renamed Mathmos: 1992. The Real Story: The company that makes the original lava lamps changed its name to Mathmos in 1992, right as lava lamps got popular again. It still makes them in the same English town where they've been made since 1963. Original company: Crestworth. Back In The Day: Turning the big light off and the lava lamp on was how you set the mood in the 90s, for a sleepover or a sad song. This tall one glows like a campfire, and the whole room looks like the inside of a fruit roll-up. Made in: Poole, Dorset, England. Word On The Playground: Fell asleep watching it once. Woke up still watching it. Original 1963 model: The Astro.
ts-pokebox: Pokémon bin. Collectibles, 1998. Childhood Pro Tip: Lent your cousin the Charizard? That's not a loan. That's a goodbye. Pokémon Red/Blue (US): September 28, 1998. The Real Story: Pokémon Red and Blue came to the US in September 1998, right after the cartoon. The cards came a few months later and took over every playground. Lots of schools banned them by the end of 1999 because of trading fights. Original Pokémon: 151. Back In The Day: In 1999 Pokémon was everything: the cards, the cartoon after school, the Game Boy game and the toys in Burger King kids' meals. This bin has the card binders, a Pikachu that talks when you squeeze it too hard and the box the Game Boy game came in. The Charizard is not in here. Anime (US debut): September 1998. Word On The Playground: Nobody knows where the Charizard went. Ask your cousin. Trading card game (US): January 9, 1999.
ts-magazines: Magazine bin. Game magazines, 1988, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Cut out the cheat codes and tape them inside the game box. Then you'll never lose the magazine page again. Nintendo Power first issue: July/August 1988. The Real Story: Nintendo Power came out in 1988 and was where you got maps, tips and cheat codes. The most famous code was up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A, Start, which gave you 30 lives in Contra. Konami Code creator: Kazuhisa Hashimoto. Back In The Day: Before the internet, game magazines were how you learned secrets. Kids passed them around at school and copied codes onto notebook paper. The back pages had ads for sea-monkeys and X-ray glasses, and we did fill out the sea-monkey form. Contra code bonus: 30 lives. Word On The Playground: Sea-Monkeys did not look like the ad. At all. The poster in the middle was pulled out the day it came. Sea-Monkeys: Brine shrimp, marketed by Harold von Braunhut from 1962.
shelf: The game closet. Board games, 1935, Parker Brothers. Childhood Pro Tip: Count the pieces before you start a game, not after. Then you'll know the missing one isn't your fault. Monopoly by Parker Brothers: 1935. The Real Story: Monopoly has been sold since 1935. It was based on an older game from 1904 that was made to show why monopolies are bad. Family game night meant Monopoly, Mouse Trap and Sorry!, all of them missing a few pieces. Based on: The Landlord's Game, by Lizzie Magie (patented 1904) Back In The Day: Family game night was a weekly thing in a lot of 90s houses. It started with an argument about which game and ended with somebody flipping the Monopoly board. The Christmas lights went up in 1995 and never came down. Mouse Trap: 1963, Ideal Toy Company. Word On The Playground: Half the boxes are missing pieces. The other half have pieces from other boxes. Free Parking jackpot: A house rule, not in the official rules.
gs-helmet: Bills helmet. Football helmet, 1990, 1993. Childhood Pro Tip: Playing football in the yard? Make the tree the end zone. Nobody can argue with a tree. Super Bowls: XXV, XXVI, XXVII, XXVIII. The Real Story: The Buffalo Bills went to four Super Bowls in a row in the early 90s, the only team ever to do it. They lost all four. The first one ended when the winning kick sailed just wide right. Seasons: 1990, 1993. Back In The Day: Super Bowl Sunday was a holiday in a lot of houses: chips, dip, everybody on the couch and the commercials that came out that day. Buffalo kids wore this helmet in the backyard for every big game and tackled the hedges. Head coach: Marv Levy. Word On The Playground: Football in the yard ended when somebody cried. Usually you. Four Super Bowl trips in a row. That's all we'll say. Quarterback: Jim Kelly. Super Bowl XXV: Lost 20, 19 to the Giants after a missed kick, 'wide right'
gs-smiley: Smiley lamp. Lamp, 1970s. Childhood Pro Tip: A smiley lamp is comforting until midnight. After midnight, don't make eye contact. Smiley created: 1963, by Harvey Ball. The Real Story: Harvey Ball drew the yellow smiley face in 1963. In the 70s two brothers added 'Have a nice day' and sold millions of buttons. It came back in the late 80s and 90s on everything, even bedroom lamps. 'Have a nice day' merch: Early 1970s, Bernard and Murray Spain. Back In The Day: The smiley face was everywhere in the 90s, on shirts, stickers, notebooks and lamps. This one glows all night and stares directly at the bed. Comforting when you're five. Terrifying at eleven. Back to comforting at thirty. Revival: Late 1980s and 1990s rave and pop culture. Word On The Playground: Won it at the fair along with a goldfish that lasted three days.
gs-plant: The plant. Houseplant, Somehow alive. Childhood Pro Tip: Most houseplants die from too much water, not too little. Forgetting it exists is basically the right move. Hard-to-kill picks: Pothos, snake plant, spider plant. The Real Story: Tough houseplants like pothos and snake plants can live through almost anything, which is why they survive kids' rooms. NASA once tested plants for cleaning the air, but you'd need a jungle to make a real difference. Pothos nickname: Devil's ivy, because it's so hard to kill. Back In The Day: Every 90s house had a plant somebody brought home from the grocery store and nobody ever watered. This one lives in a kid's room, next to the game closet, and it is somehow thriving. Science can't explain it. NASA Clean Air Study: 1989. Word On The Playground: Got the leftover Kool-Aid once. Grew an inch.
gs-lights: The string lights. String lights, 1882. Childhood Pro Tip: Bulb out on the strand? Test the dark ones one by one with a good bulb. Bring snacks. It's a while. First electric tree lights: 1882, Edward H. Johnson. The Real Story: The first electric Christmas tree lights were put up in 1882 by a friend of Thomas Edison, with 80 red, white and blue bulbs. On older strands, one dead bulb makes the whole string go dark, so you had to test every bulb. Bulbs on that tree: 80, red, white and blue. Back In The Day: Putting up Christmas lights was a family job. Somebody untangled the strand on the living room floor, somebody held the ladder and somebody yelled "Try it now!" These went up in 1995 and never came down, because the room just looked better. Series wiring: One bad bulb can kill the whole strand. Word On The Playground: Unplug them at night or they "start fires" (they never started fires). Modern fix: Shunts let current pass a dead bulb.
dresser: The dresser. Furniture, Sticker museum. Childhood Pro Tip: Hide your stuff in the sock drawer, under the socks you never wear. Nobody looks there, not even you. Bottom drawer: Clothes. The Real Story: The dresser kept clothes in the bottom drawers and secrets in the top one. In a lot of 90s houses it was also covered in stickers from magazines, cereal boxes and the book fair. Those stickers never come all the way off. Top drawer: Anything important. Back In The Day: Nobody was allowed to put stickers on the furniture. We put stickers on the furniture. In a lot of 90s rooms, the dresser was basically a history book: Mario, Yoshi, No Fear and a smiley face that won't come off. Sticker removal: Hair dryer heat helps; patience mostly doesn't. Word On The Playground: The top drawer never closed all the way.
dr-stickers: Mario and Yoshi stickers. Stickers, 1988, Nintendo. Childhood Pro Tip: Peeling a sticker halfway is the worst choice. Commit. Leave it, or lose it forever. Mario's debut: Donkey Kong (1981), as 'Jumpman' The Real Story: Mario first showed up in Donkey Kong in 1981, where he was called Jumpman. By the 90s Nintendo characters were on everything, and Nintendo Power came with posters and stickers. The magazine ran until 2012. Created by: Shigeru Miyamoto. Back In The Day: Stickers came free in magazines, cereal boxes and at the doctor's office, and kids put them on everything. These went straight onto the dresser before anybody could stop it. They've survived three moves and one very hard scrubbing. Nintendo Power run: 1988, 2012. Word On The Playground: Peeling one off halfway and then putting it back was worse than leaving it. Yoshi's debut: Super Mario World (1990)
dr-nofear: No Fear sticker. Sticker, 1989. Childhood Pro Tip: No Fear means no fear. Except of Mom finding the sticker on the dresser. That's normal fear. Founded: 1989. The Real Story: No Fear started in 1989 in Southern California, from the dirt bike racing crowd. Its shirts had big tough sayings about winning, and by the mid-90s the logo was everywhere: shirts, stickers and car windows. Founders: Mark Simo, Brian Simo, Marty Moates. Back In The Day: No Fear shirts were the cool shirts in the 90s, with sayings like "Second place is the first loser" across the back. We thought that was deep. Some schools even banned the shirts, which only made them cooler. Roots: Motocross and racing. Word On The Playground: Fear: medium. Known for: Slogan T-shirts and stickers.
clutterdesk: The homework desk. Desk, Homework was never done here. Childhood Pro Tip: Do your homework the minute you get home. Then the rest of the day is yours. Nobody ever followed this advice. Modern LEGO brick: Patented 1958. The Real Story: The desk was for homework, officially. Really it was for LEGO, drawing, snacks and games. The LEGO brick we know came out in 1958, and by the 90s every desk drawer had a few loose ones. LEGO founded: 1932, by Ole Kirk Christiansen, Denmark. Back In The Day: After school, the routine was a snack, cartoons, and "homework" at the desk. This desk was used for building LEGO, drawing, eating pizza rolls, playing Super Nintendo with the sound off and hiding the report card. Homework happened on the bus. Name: From Danish 'leg godt,' meaning 'play well' Word On The Playground: Every drawer is a junk drawer. The stickers are load-bearing.
cd-lava: Desk lava lamp. Lava lamp, 1963. Childhood Pro Tip: Keep crayons, gum and anything wax far away from the lava lamp base. It gets hot enough to melt them. Heat comes from: A light bulb in the base. The Real Story: A lava lamp is just a bulb under a bottle of liquid and wax. The heat makes the wax rise, it cools off at the top, and it sinks again, over and over. The base gets really hot, so don't touch it. Idea came from: An egg timer bubbling on a stove. Back In The Day: A lava lamp on a homework desk was supposed to help you focus. Instead you spent the next hour naming the blobs. That one's Gary. Gary just split into two Garys. The base gets: Hot. Very hot. Word On The Playground: Lost one blue crayon to science. It's still stuck to the base.
cd-cup: Smiley pencil cup. Pencil cup, Full of pens that don't work. Childhood Pro Tip: Pen not writing? Scribble on the back of your hand or a rubber eraser to get the ink going. Works most of the time. Gel pen invented: 1984, Sakura Color Products. The Real Story: Gel pens were invented in Japan in 1984, and the glitter, milky and scented ones were all over 90s schools. Clicky pens are older: Parker's Jotter came out in 1954. Somebody always borrowed your best one. Famous line: Gelly Roll. Back In The Day: Gel pens took over schools in the late 90s: glitter, milky, scented, the works. Kids traded them and wrote notes in every color. Somehow this cup has twenty pens and not one of them writes, except the grape-scented gel pen at the bottom. Parker Jotter: 1954. Word On The Playground: Click pens: clicked eight thousand times during tests. 90s favorites: Glitter, milky and scented inks.
cd-tapes: Video game tape stack. Rental tapes, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Friday night rental trick: get there right after school. By seven o'clock every copy of the new game is gone. Blockbuster founded: 1985, Dallas, Texas. The Real Story: You rented movies and video games from the video store, and Blockbuster was the biggest one. It started in 1985 and had about 9,000 stores by 2004, then streaming took over. One store is still open, in Bend, Oregon. Founder: David Cook. Back In The Day: Renting was how you tried new games. Walking the aisles at the video store on a Friday night, picking one game for the weekend, and then begging for one more day. A couple of these still have the store's sticker on the case. Peak: About 9,000 stores (2004) Word On The Playground: The late fee is now worth more than the store. Blockbuster night was a Friday-night ritual. Last store: Bend, Oregon. Most feared phrase: Late fee.
cd-car: Red sports car. Die-cast car, 1953. Childhood Pro Tip: Car noises must be made with your mouth. The louder the noise, the faster the car. Facts. Matchbox launched: 1953, by Lesney Products (UK) The Real Story: Tiny metal toy cars took off in 1953 when a man made one small enough to fit in a matchbox for his daughter, and Matchbox was born. Mattel answered with Hot Wheels in 1968. Hot Wheels launched: 1968, by Mattel. Back In The Day: Every kid had a dream car picked out by age ten, usually red and usually Italian. Posters of sports cars went on the wall next to the basketball players. This one does laps around the pencil cup until you can buy the real one. Common scale: About 1:64. Word On The Playground: Engine noises: done with your mouth, very loud.
cd-clock: Clock radio. Clock radio, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Don't know how to change the alarm? Leave it. You're now an early riser. Congratulations. Common snooze: About 9 minutes. The Real Story: Clock radios had an alarm, a clock and a radio, with a big snooze button for slapping in the dark. Snooze usually gave you nine more minutes. Setting the time meant holding a button while the numbers raced by. Display: Red LED digits. Back In The Day: Lots of kids had a paper route in the 90s, up before school to toss newspapers onto porches for a few dollars a week. The alarm got set for paper route time once, as a business plan. The business lasted a week. The alarm stayed at 5:41 for another year. Setting it: Hold a button while the numbers race by. Word On The Playground: Hitting the snooze button blind in the dark is a skill.
cd-phone: Brick phone. Cell phone, 1983. Childhood Pro Tip: Snake gets faster as it grows. Stay near the edges and turn early. That's how the high scores were made. First handheld cell phone: Motorola DynaTAC 8000X, 1983. The Real Story: The first cell phone you could buy came out in 1983, cost $3,995, and was so big people called it 'the brick.' Phones got much smaller in the 90s, and in 1997 Nokia added Snake, one of the first famous phone games. Launch price: $3,995. Back In The Day: Cell phones in the 90s were for grown-ups and emergencies. Calls cost money by the minute, so kids barely got to touch one. This was Mom's old phone, "only for emergencies". Twenty minutes of Snake counted as an emergency, right? Snake debut: Nokia 6110, 1997. Word On The Playground: Ringtone: composed yourself, note by note, one awful afternoon. The antenna pulled out. It did nothing. You pulled it out anyway. Snake creator: Taneli Armanto.
cd-pogs: POGs. Milk caps, Early 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Never play for keeps. If you do play for keeps, bring the skull slammer and no feelings. Name comes from: POG juice: Passion fruit, Orange, Guava. The Real Story: POG was a juice from Hawaii: Passion fruit, Orange and Guava. A teacher there brought back an old game of flipping the bottle caps in 1991, and by the mid-90s every school had it. Stack the caps, throw the slammer, keep what flips. Juice created: 1971, by Mary Soon for Haleakala Dairy. Back In The Day: POGs swept through schools in the mid-90s. Kids carried them in plastic tubes and played at recess, and a lot of schools banned them after kids lost whole collections playing "for keeps". The heavy slammer on top is the one that won all these. Game revived: 1991, Hawaii. Word On The Playground: The skull slammer was the most powerful object in the cafeteria. Named after a juice. Nobody drank the juice. Peak craze: Early to mid-1990s. Slammer: A heavier cap, often plastic or metal.
cd-sketch: The sketchbook (and the Cool S) Doodle, Graffiti letters, every page. Childhood Pro Tip: Cool S: three lines on top, three on the bottom, then connect them. A minute to learn, a lifetime to master. Also called: Stussy S, Superman S, Pointy S. The Real Story: The 'Cool S' was drawn on every notebook in every school, and nobody knows who started it. It's made from two rows of three lines, which is why so many kids figured it out on their own. Inventor: Unknown. Back In The Day: Doodling in the margins was a 90s art form. Every notebook had the same things: the Cool S, a 3D cube, bubble letters and a dragon that doesn't look like a dragon. Nobody taught it. Everybody knew it. Construction: Two rows of three parallel lines, then connect. Word On The Playground: Back page: fake signatures, practicing for the report card. Everybody drew the S. Nobody knows who invented the S.
cd-lamp: Desk lamp. Desk lamp, Burns fingers on contact. Childhood Pro Tip: Old desk lamps double as interrogation lights. Point it at your little brother and ask where the remote went. Incandescent waste: About 90% of energy becomes heat. The Real Story: Old light bulbs turned most of their power into heat instead of light, which is why desk lamps burned your fingers. The bendy desk lamp design comes from the 1930s. Cooler LED bulbs have mostly taken over. Balanced-arm lamp: Anglepoise, George Carwardine, 1930s. Back In The Day: Old light bulbs got hot. Really hot. The desk lamp kept your hands warm during winter homework, and once, as a test, a Hot Pocket. We did not try that. Okay, we tried that. Replaced by: Compact fluorescents, then LEDs. Word On The Playground: Burned a finger on the shade at least once a year. Moths found it every summer night.
cd-frog: Little green guy. Meal toy, 1979. Childhood Pro Tip: The toy is the meal. The food is just packaging. Every kid knows this. Happy Meal launched: 1979, nationwide in the US. The Real Story: McDonald's started the Happy Meal across the US in 1979, and the toy inside became the real reason kids wanted one. Burger King and others followed. The biggest 90s toy craze was Teenie Beanie Babies in 1997. Biggest 90s craze: Teenie Beanie Babies, 1997. Back In The Day: Kids' meals came with a toy, and the toys changed every few weeks, so you begged to go back until you had the whole set. This little guy came free with one. Worth more than the meal. He's been the desk lamp's security guard ever since. Value: Higher than the meal, emotionally. Word On The Playground: Had a name once. Nobody remembers it.
cd-8ball: Magic 8 Ball. Fortune toy, 1950. Childhood Pro Tip: If the Magic 8 Ball says no, shake it again. Keep shaking until it agrees. That's how science works. Came out: Around 1950. The Real Story: The Magic 8 Ball came out around 1950. Shake it, flip it, and a floating answer shows up in the window. Inside is a 20-sided shape in blue liquid with 10 yes answers, 5 no answers and 5 maybes. Inside: A 20-sided shape floating in blue liquid. Back In The Day: The Magic 8 Ball was the sleepover question machine. Kids passed it around the circle asking about crushes, tests and if it would snow tomorrow. Asked it if you'd pass the spelling test. It said "Outlook not so good". It was right. Answers: 10 yes, 5 maybe, 5 no. Word On The Playground: Asked if your crush liked you back. It said "Ask again later". It's been later for a long time. Owned by: Mattel.
cd-photo: The photo. School photo, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Picture day trick: think of something funny right before the flash. It beats the smile from the mirror. Lifetouch founded: 1936. The Real Story: Picture day meant a laser background, a free plastic comb, and tiny wallet photos to trade with friends. Companies like Lifetouch took millions of school pictures every year. Retake day was a second chance that rarely helped. 90s look: Laser backgrounds. Back In The Day: School picture day meant your nicest shirt, a laser background, and a photographer combing your hair with the same comb as everyone else. Then you traded wallet-size photos with friends and wrote on the back. Package staple: Wallet-size prints. Word On The Playground: The retake was somehow worse. Practiced a smile in the mirror for a week. Blinked. Free gift: A plastic comb.
cd-tmnt: Ninja Turtles cup. Cup, 1990. Childhood Pro Tip: A plastic movie cup makes a perfect marker holder. It also holds the smell of Sprite forever. Fair trade. First movie: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, March 1990. The Real Story: Turtle mania was huge: the cartoon started in 1987 and the first live-action movie came out in 1990, with turtle suits made by Jim Henson's team. Turtles were on cups, cereal and toys, and pizza places loved them. Turtle suits: Jim Henson's Creature Shop. Back In The Day: Pizza places and fast food spots sold big plastic cups with movie and cartoon characters on them, and kids collected the whole set. This one came with a large pizza and a toy that broke in the car. It holds markers now. Movie theme: 'Turtle Power!' by Partners in Kryme. Word On The Playground: Turtle Power. Smells faintly of Sprite and a little like pizza. Favorite food: Pizza.
cd-walkman: Walkman. Cassette player, 1979, Sony. Childhood Pro Tip: Save batteries: rewind tapes with a pencil in the hole. Spin it fast. Your wrist will survive. First model: TPS-L2, July 1, 1979. The Real Story: Sony's first Walkman came out in 1979 and let you carry your music anywhere. Later ones could flip the tape for you, called auto-reverse. Sony sold about 220 million tape Walkmans before stopping in 2010. Auto-reverse: Added in 1982. Back In The Day: Bus rides and long car trips were a whole movie with headphones on. Kids carried a little case of tapes and swapped them with friends. The foam earpieces were orange once. Now they're a color science doesn't have a name for. Cassette Walkmans sold: About 220 million. Word On The Playground: The tape got eaten right at the best part. Every time. Sharing one pair of headphones, one ear each. Cassette production ended: 2010 (Japan)
cd-snes: Donkey Kong Country cartridge. SNES game, 1994, Rare. Childhood Pro Tip: Donkey Kong Country secret: on the game select screen, press B, A, R, R, A, L for 50 lives. Came out: November 1994. The Real Story: Donkey Kong Country came out for the Super Nintendo in 1994. The team built the characters on powerful computers first, so the game looked way better than anything else on the system. It sold over 9 million copies. Made by: Rare, a game studio in England. Back In The Day: Christmas morning 1994. Unwrapped, plugged in, played until the TV got hot. Donkey Kong Country looked like nothing else on the Super Nintendo, and the minecart levels made grown-ups throw controllers. This cartridge has seen things. The look: Built as 3D models first, then turned into game art. Word On The Playground: Blowing on Super Nintendo carts did nothing either. We did it anyway. Sold: 9.3 million copies.
cd-yoyo: Yo-yo. Yo-yo, 1929, Duncan. Childhood Pro Tip: String twisted? Let the yo-yo hang and spin until it straightens. Then practice 'walk the dog' away from the dog. Pedro Flores Yo-yo Company: 1928, Santa Barbara. The Real Story: Yo-yos took off in America in the 1920s and 30s when Duncan sent yo-yo pros to schools to show off tricks and run contests. The 90s had its own yo-yo craze, done the same way. Duncan: Took over in the early 1930s. Back In The Day: The yo-yo guy came to school, did tricks in the gym and everybody bought one that afternoon. For a few months the whole playground was yo-yos. "Around the world" hit the lamp. "Rock the baby" tied the string into a knot that's still in there. Classic tricks: Walk the Dog, Around the World, Rock the Baby. Word On The Playground: "Walk the dog" actually hit the dog. Marketing secret: Touring yo-yo demonstrators.
cd-sonic: Sonic tape. VHS tape, 1991, Sega. Childhood Pro Tip: Sonic or Mario? Say 'both' and you'll be fine. Say 'Mario' at the wrong lunch table and you won't. Game released: June 23, 1991 (Genesis) The Real Story: Sega made Sonic the Hedgehog in 1991 to take on Mario. Two Sonic cartoons came out in 1993: a silly one where he loved chili dogs, and a more serious Saturday morning one. Creators: Yuji Naka and Naoto Ohshima. Back In The Day: Sega vs Nintendo was the real war of the 90s. Kids picked a side, and the TV ads picked fights too. Sonic had two cartoons on Saturday mornings, taped and watched again on Sunday. This desk was Switzerland: both of them lived here. Cartoons: Two Sonic series debuted in 1993. Word On The Playground: Chili dogs became the only acceptable food for a month. Favorite food: Chili dogs. Rival: Mario.
cd-vhs: The movie row. VHS tape, 1996, Warner Bros. Childhood Pro Tip: To dunk like Michael Jordan, lower the hoop to four feet. Then tell everyone it was regulation. Released: November 15, 1996. The Real Story: Space Jam (1996) put Michael Jordan on a basketball team with Bugs Bunny and the Looney Tunes against aliens called the Monstars. It was the number one movie when it came out, and the soundtrack was everywhere. Director: Joe Pytka. Back In The Day: Space Jam came out in 1996 and every kid wanted to be Michael Jordan. Mini hoops went up on closet doors everywhere. The Space Jam soundtrack lived in the Walkman for a year. Stars: Michael Jordan and the Looney Tunes. Word On The Playground: Monstars were the scariest villains ever made, change my mind. Worldwide gross: About $250 million. Villains: The Monstars.
cd-trophy: Participation trophy. Trophy, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Losing every game still gets a trophy. Keep losing with confidence. The trophy doesn't know. Tee-ball ages: Usually about 4 to 7. The Real Story: Tee-ball, where you hit the ball off a stand instead of a pitch, was the first sport for a lot of little kids. Many leagues gave every player a trophy at the end of the season, win or lose. Trophy style: Gold-colored plastic figure on a base. Back In The Day: Saturday mornings in spring meant tee-ball. Parents in folding chairs, a snack schedule on the fridge and juice boxes after the game. This team lost every single game and everybody got a trophy anyway. It is the proudest thing on this desk. Best part of the game: Orange slices. Word On The Playground: Orange slices at halftime were the actual reason anybody played.
cd-stickers: Drawer stickers. Stickers, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Charge glow-in-the-dark stickers with a flashlight right before bed. Then immediately fall asleep and miss it. Old glow stickers: Faded in a few minutes. The Real Story: Glow-in-the-dark stickers soak up light and slowly give it back in the dark. Older ones faded fast. New ones from the 90s glowed brighter and much longer. Skater and surf stickers were a whole other collection. 90s glow stickers: Glowed bright for much longer. Back In The Day: Every drawer has a sticker from a different phase: the skater phase, the space phase, the No Fear phase. In the 90s, the stickers on your stuff told everybody who you were trying to be. Charge them with: Any bright light. Word On The Playground: The planet sticker glows if the lights were on long enough.
cd-chair: The spinny chair. Desk chair, Mission control. Childhood Pro Tip: Spin until dizzy. Spin back the other way to cancel it out. This does not work. Spin anyway. Early swivel chair: Credited to Thomas Jefferson, 1776. The Real Story: Thomas Jefferson is said to have used a spinning chair while writing the Declaration of Independence. Rolling desk chairs became normal in offices later, and kids found out they're perfect for hallway races. Wheels pioneer: Charles Darwin (by legend) Back In The Day: The spinny chair was the best seat in the house, and every kid with one tested how fast it could go. The cushion has a hole that grows a little every year. It still rolls perfectly to the TV. Best use: Hallway races. Word On The Playground: Office chair races down the hallway. Banned.
desk: The family computer. Home computer, 1998. Childhood Pro Tip: Downloading something big? Tape a sign to every phone in the house: DO NOT PICK UP. Windows 98 released: June 25, 1998. The Real Story: In the late 90s a lot of families shared one computer and got online through the phone line. Windows 98 came out in 1998. If anyone picked up the phone, the internet hung up on you. Top dial-up speed: 56 kilobits a second (V.90 standard, 1998) Back In The Day: The family computer sat in the corner and the whole house took turns. A kitchen timer decided whose turn it was. Kids did homework in Encarta, played games, and waited an hour for one song to download. Connection sound: The modem handshake screech. Word On The Playground: That dial-up screech meant you were about to be online. "Get off the internet, I need to use the phone!" Biggest threat: Someone picking up the phone.
pc-monitor: Beige CRT monitor. CRT monitor, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Leave a screensaver on when you walk away. It isn't just for fun. It keeps the picture from burning into the screen. Common sizes: 14 and 15 inches. The Real Story: Computer screens in the 90s were big beige boxes with a tube inside, just like TVs. A 15-inch one only showed about 14 inches of picture. They were heavy, they hummed, and they zapped you with static. Picture you could see: About 14 inches on a 15-inch screen. Back In The Day: Starting the computer took a while. The Windows logo came up and you waited, and waited, and then the desktop showed up and you waited some more. Kids changed the wallpaper the first day and then forgot about it for a whole year. Screensavers: Made so a picture left on too long wouldn't burn into the screen. Word On The Playground: 3D Pipes screensaver, for hours. Heavier than you were.
pc-tower: The tower. PC tower, 1993, Intel. Childhood Pro Tip: Press the Turbo button. Nothing happens. Feel faster anyway. Pentium launch: March 22, 1993. The Real Story: Intel's Pentium chip came out in 1993, and the 'Intel Inside' sticker ended up on millions of beige computers. The Turbo button was confusing: it mostly slowed the computer down so old games wouldn't run too fast. 'Intel Inside' campaign: Started 1991. Back In The Day: A beige box under the desk was the most expensive thing in a lot of 90s houses. It came with a CD tray that kids used as a cup holder at least once, and a sticker on the front that seemed more important than anything inside. Turbo button: Really a 'slow down' button for old software. Word On The Playground: Pressing the power button and hearing every fan wake up. 1994 headline: The Pentium FDIV math bug.
pc-printer: Inkjet printer. Inkjet printer, 1988. Childhood Pro Tip: Out of color ink? Print the cover page in black and white and call it 'artistic.' HP DeskJet launch: 1988. The Real Story: HP's DeskJet printers, starting in 1988, made color printing cheap enough for home. Before that, printers used long paper with holes down the sides, great for banners. Running out of one ink color the night before a project was a classic. Before inkjets: Dot-matrix printers. Back In The Day: Printing a school report was an event. You hit Print and listened to it go one slow line at a time while the whole house heard it. Most reports got printed the night before they were due. Holey paper: Continuous tractor-feed paper for dot-matrix printers. Word On The Playground: It jammed every single time it was the night before. Banner software: The Print Shop, 1984.
pc-keyboard: Clicky keyboard. Keyboard, 1987. Childhood Pro Tip: Home row is A, S, D, F and J, K, L, semicolon. Feel for the little bumps on F and J and you'll never have to look down. Mavis Beacon released: 1987. The Real Story: Mavis Beacon Teaches Typing came out in 1987 and was how kids learned to type. Fun fact: Mavis wasn't a real person. The woman on the box was a model. Old IBM keyboards were loud, clicky and nearly unbreakable. Mavis is: A fictional character. Back In The Day: Lots of schools had computer class in the 90s, with a whole lab of beige computers and typing games. Kids learned to type there, and then got really fast at home typing instant messages late at night. Cover model: Renée L'Espérance. Word On The Playground: Crumbs between the keys. All of them. Loud enough to wake the house at midnight. IBM Model M: 1985, buckling-spring keys.
pc-mouse: Ball mouse. Ball mouse, 1972. Childhood Pro Tip: Cursor skipping? Pop out the ball, scrape the rollers with a fingernail, and never discuss the gunk. First mouse: 1964, Douglas Engelbart's team at SRI. The Real Story: The first computer mouse was a wooden box with wheels, built in 1964. Later mice used a rolling ball underneath, and the rollers inside always got gunked up. Light-based mice replaced them around 2000. Ball mouse: 1972, Bill English at Xerox PARC. Back In The Day: Kids learned the mouse playing Solitaire and Minesweeper, and the family computer had a free mouse pad from a bank or a store. Double-clicking was a skill that took grown-ups years. Replaced by: Optical mice, around 1999, 2000s. Word On The Playground: The mouse pad was a free one from a bank. Grandma clicked once and waited. Every time. Maintenance: Clean the ball and the rollers.
pc-cds: CD-ROMs and floppies. Software, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Free AOL CDs make great coasters, mirrors and ninja stars. Only one of those is allowed. A floppy held: 1.44 megabytes, about one song. The Real Story: Software used to come on floppy disks, and Windows 95 needed 13 of them. CDs held way more, about as much as 450 floppies, so they took over. AOL mailed free trial discs to basically every house in America. A CD held: About 650 megabytes, like 450 floppies. Back In The Day: Encyclopedias came on CD in the 90s, so school reports started with Encarta instead of the big books at the library. Demo discs came in cereal boxes and magazines, and the free AOL discs showed up in the mail almost every week. Windows 95 on floppies: 13 disks. Word On The Playground: 1,000 free hours! (must be used within one month). AOL offers: Free hours, mailed to every house.
pc-pencils: Pencil cup. Colored pencils, Every colour but the one you need. Childhood Pro Tip: Hide the blue pencil before the state project. Everyone needs the ocean. Supply and demand. Pencil 'lead': Graphite and clay, no lead at all. The Real Story: There's no lead in a pencil. It's graphite mixed with clay. People called it lead hundreds of years ago, when they found graphite in England and thought it was lead. Colored pencils use colored wax instead. Name comes from: People in the 1500s mixing up graphite and lead. Back In The Day: State projects, science fair posters and book report covers were all colored in pencil. Every class had one kid with the 64-pack, and everybody was nice to that kid. Somebody always took the blue. Colored pencils: Color mixed with wax. Word On The Playground: Electric pencil sharpeners: ate half the pencil every time.
pc-stickers: Drawer stickers. Stickers, 1981, MTV. Childhood Pro Tip: Put the sticker on the inside of the drawer. Mom never checks in there, and it lasts forever. Launched: August 1, 1981. The Real Story: MTV started on August 1, 1981, playing music videos all day. By the 90s it had shows like The Real World and TRL, and the logo was on notebooks, stickers and shirts everywhere. First video: 'Video Killed the Radio Star,' The Buggles. Back In The Day: Every drawer got a sticker the day you got it. Free stickers came with magazines, CDs and every trip to the mall. Peeling them off now would take the paint with them, so they stay. Real World premiere: 1992. Word On The Playground: The drawer with the RAD sticker is where the good stuff is hidden. TRL premiere: 1998.
pc-games: PC game boxes. PC games, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Read the whole manual while the game installs. You've got an hour. Learn the backstory of every elf. Myst released: 1993. The Real Story: 90s computer games came in huge boxes with thick manuals and maps, even though the disc was tiny. Myst (1993) was the best-selling computer game until The Sims in 2002. The big boxes went away in the early 2000s. Myst developer: Cyan. Back In The Day: Computer games were sold in big boxes on shelves at the electronics store, and kids picked them by the picture on the front. The system requirements on the back were a test your computer never quite passed. Myst's record: Best-selling PC game until The Sims (2002) Word On The Playground: Installing took an hour. Worth it. Big box extras: Manuals, maps, posters, 'feelies'
gushers: Fruit Gushers. Fruit snack, 1991, Betty Crocker. Childhood Pro Tip: Freeze your Gushers overnight. The juice turns into a cold little slush and they last way longer. Introduced: 1991. The Real Story: Fruit Gushers came out in 1991: chewy fruit snacks with juice inside. The first flavors were strawberry and grape. The commercials showed kids' heads turning into fruit after one bite. That never happened. We checked. Brand: Betty Crocker (General Mills) Back In The Day: Lunch tables in the 90s worked like a stock market. One pack of Gushers could buy two Fruit Roll-Ups and a Capri Sun, or one pudding cup if the market was bad. Everybody's lunch box was open for business. Original flavors: Strawberry Splash and Gushin' Grape. Word On The Playground: Gushers were worth more than money in the cafeteria. The commercial said your head would turn into a fruit. Still waiting. Big comeback: Watermelon returned in 2024 by fan demand.
cards: Pokémon cards. Trading cards, 1999, Wizards of the Coast. Childhood Pro Tip: Put your best cards in plastic sleeves and keep them out of your back pocket. Bent cards lose all their trade value. US release: January 9, 1999. The Real Story: Pokémon cards hit the US on January 9, 1999. The first set had 102 cards, 16 of them shiny, and the shiny Charizard was the card every kid wanted. First-edition ones are now worth a fortune. Publisher (US): Wizards of the Coast. Back In The Day: In 1999 every recess was a trading floor. Kids carried binders to school, traded doubles at lunch, and argued over who got the better deal. The pile on the floor here is the trade pile. The holographic Charizard was traded for a bike, and that is a decision we live with. Cards in set: 102. Word On The Playground: Rubber bands ruined everything. Banned at school after the "it's mine, you traded it" incident. Holographic Pokémon: 16. Most wanted: Charizard, #4/102.
hotpockets: Hot Pockets and pizza rolls. Frozen snack, 1983, Chef America. Childhood Pro Tip: Hot Pocket strategy: let it sit one whole minute after the microwave. The middle stops being frozen. Hot Pockets introduced: 1983. The Real Story: Hot Pockets came out in 1983, made by two brothers, and the crispy sleeve was the big idea. Pizza rolls are older, from 1968, and became Totino's in 1993. Both burned the roof of your mouth. Both were worth it. Hot Pockets creators: Paul and David Merage. Back In The Day: After school in the 90s, a lot of kids made their own snack while their parents were still at work. The microwave was the kitchen. Two minutes: lava on the outside, still frozen in the middle. Pizza rolls were worse, a tiny pocket of sun in every bite. We never learned. Sold to Nestlé: 2002, for $2.6 billion. Word On The Playground: The crisping sleeve did nothing and we all knew it. Eaten on the floor because the desk was full and the table was "for grown-ups". Pizza rolls created: 1968, by Jeno's Inc. (developed by Beatrice Ojakangas) Rebranded Totino's: 1993.
