jordans: The high-tops. Sneakers, 1985, Nike. Childhood Pro Tip: New sneakers rule: stuff the toes with socks so they don't crease. Clean the soles with a toothbrush. First Air Jordan: 1985. The Real Story: Nike signed Michael Jordan and made the first Air Jordans in 1985. They became the most famous sneakers ever. Kids saved up for months, and a crease in the toe felt like the end of the world. Air Jordan 1 designer: Peter Moore. Back In The Day: Saved birthday money for six months for these. In the 90s, new sneakers came out on Saturdays, and kids lined up at the mall before it opened. Wore them once outside, got a scuff, and they've lived on the floor by the shelf ever since, toes pointed out like they're on display. Because they are. Air Jordan III: 1988, Tinker Hatfield. Word On The Playground: Pump them up, lace them tight, look fresh. Brand: Jordan Brand (Nike)
car: RC trucks. RC trucks, 1990s. Childhood Pro Tip: Batteries not included means no fun on Christmas morning. Ask for a pack of batteries on your list too. Trust us. The problem: Two trucks on the same signal, one remote drives both. The Real Story: Cheap remote control trucks were a top Christmas gift in the 80s and 90s. Many used the same radio signal, so your remote could steer your friend's truck. Batteries were never included. Power: AA or 9-volt batteries, never included. Back In The Day: Christmas morning: three RC trucks and zero batteries in the whole house. Most stores were closed, so you had to wait until the next day. Then they drove under the bed and didn't come out for three years. Word On The Playground: Racing a friend meant both remotes drove both trucks. Chaos.
hotwheels: Hot Wheels track. Toy track, 1968, Mattel. Childhood Pro Tip: Car flying off the loop? Start it higher. Speed holds it in. A stack of books makes a great hill. Launched: 1968. The Real Story: Mattel made Hot Wheels in 1968, with bright orange track you could snap into loops, jumps and long ramps. Kids built tracks across whole houses. Hot Wheels became one of the best-selling toys of all time. Maker: Mattel. Back In The Day: It started as one loop. Then the track went off the toy shelf, under the bed, across the hallway and down the stairs, held together with tape and a dictionary for the jump. Building track all over the house was a whole Saturday plan. Driving force: Mattel co-founder Elliot Handler. Word On The Playground: The orange track doubled as a sword, a whip and the thing Mom swore she'd throw out. Zero to sixty in one flick of the finger. Sixty to under the couch forever. Only the slow, ugly station wagon ever made it all the way through the loop. Famous track color: Orange. First cars: The 'Sweet Sixteen'
army: Army men. Toy soldiers, 1950s. Childhood Pro Tip: Never step on army men barefoot. If you do, the bazooka guy was obviously aiming for you. Made of: Cheap molded plastic. The Real Story: Green plastic army men became a cheap bag-of-toys classic after World War II, when plastic replaced old metal toy soldiers. Toy Story made them famous all over again in 1995. Before plastic: Toy soldiers were made of metal. Back In The Day: A bag of army men cost about a dollar, and one bag gave you a whole war. Battles went across the carpet, the bed and the bathtub, and the losers got flicked. The guy lying down with the rifle could never stand up for anything. Movie fame: Sarge and his troops in Toy Story, 1995. Word On The Playground: Stepping on one barefoot is worse than LEGO. Fight us. The parachute guys never once landed where you threw them.
ispy-book: I Spy. Picture book, 1992, Scholastic. Childhood Pro Tip: Stuck on a page? Turn the book upside down. Your eyes stop seeing the picture and start seeing the shapes. First published: 1992. The Real Story: I Spy came out in 1992 with rhyming riddles by Jean Marzollo and photos by Walter Wick. Every page was built by hand from real toys and things, then photographed. No computers. The series sold tens of millions. Riddles by: Jean Marzollo. Back In The Day: Every Scholastic book fair it was right there on the front table, shrink-wrapped, $12.95, and you had exactly 85 cents and a pencil topper. So you checked it out from the school library instead. Then you checked it out again. This copy still has the library pocket glued in the front. The due date says October 1998. Photographs by: Walter Wick. Word On The Playground: Somebody always circled the answers in pen, so every library copy was already half solved. The riddles rhyme, so you read them in a sing-song voice whether you wanted to or not. Late fee is ten cents a day. It has been a while. The librarian has not forgotten. How the pages were made: Real objects arranged and photographed. Format: Rhyming riddles.
furby: Furby. Robot toy, 1998, Tiger Electronics. Childhood Pro Tip: Furby can't be turned off. To get some sleep, put it somewhere dark and quiet, and it will go to sleep too. Mostly. Launched: October 2, 1998. The Real Story: Furby came out in October 1998 for about $35. It spoke its own language, Furbish, and seemed to learn English over time, but the words were already inside it. It sold millions, and the NSA banned it from its offices just in case. Inventors: Dave Hampton and Caleb Chung. Back In The Day: Furby was the toy of Christmas 1998. Stores sold out, parents waited in line before the doors opened, and some people paid hundreds of dollars for one. Mom stood in line at 6 a.m. for this one, and a lady in the next aisle offered her a hundred dollars for it. Price: About $35. Word On The Playground: It says "me sleepy" in a dark closet at 3 a.m. anyway. Two Furbies in the same room will talk to each other forever. Nobody knows what they're planning. Turn it upside down and it screams. Turn off the light and it snores. Basically a little brother. Somebody at school swore you could make it say a bad word. You could not. Sold: 40+ million during its original three-year run. NSA ban: 1999, later withdrawn.
poochi: Poo-Chi. Robot dog, 2000, Sega Toys. Childhood Pro Tip: Talk to Poo-Chi up close and clear. In a noisy room he ignores you, just like a real dog. Released: 2000. The Real Story: Poo-Chi was a robot puppy from Sega Toys that came out in 2000 for $24.99. He had red light-up eyes, listened to your voice, and sang songs when you pressed his head. Over 10 million sold in about eight months. Made by: Sega Toys; distributed by Tiger Electronics. Back In The Day: After the Furby craze, Poo-Chi was the cool new thing for Christmas 2000: a robot puppy whose eyes turned into hearts when he was happy. He came with his own bone, and he loved that bone more than he loved you. The box said Poo-Chis could talk to each other. Every kid on the street tried it. US price: $24.99. Word On The Playground: He sang six songs, all in beeps. His voice was a speaker the size of a dime, so a bark sounded like a calculator having feelings. Held two of them nose to nose for a whole recess, waiting for them to talk. One fell asleep. His bones are all over this room somewhere. He never could find them on his own. Sold: 10+ million in about eight months. Spin-offs: Meow-Chi, Dino-Chi, Chirpy-Chi.
armor: Action figure. Action figure, 1982, Hasbro. Childhood Pro Tip: Keep the tiny guns and backpacks in a film canister or an old Altoids tin. They'll be lost within the hour otherwise. 'Action figure' coined: 1964, by Hasbro for G.I. Joe. The Real Story: Hasbro made up the term 'action figure' in 1964 for G.I. Joe, so boys' dolls would sound tougher. In 1982 the figures got small, and each package had a card on the back with the character's code name and story. A Real American Hero: 1982. Back In The Day: Action figures were the toy aisle in the 90s: G.I. Joe, Ninja Turtles, Power Rangers, a whole wall of them. Each came with tiny gear that was all gone within the first hour. This one keeps watch over the NES now, which is a very important job. Standard size: 3¾ inches. Word On The Playground: Had a whole backstory on the card. Never read it. Gun: couch. Backpack: vacuum. Helmet: the dog. Package extra: Character file cards.
rubik: Rubik's Cube. Puzzle, 1974. Childhood Pro Tip: Solve one side, then finish the whole top layer before you touch the rest. That's how the fast kids did it. Invented: 1974, by Ernő Rubik. The Real Story: Ernő Rubik invented the cube in Hungary in 1974 and it went worldwide in 1980. It can be scrambled about 43 quintillion ways, and in 2010 people proved every one can be solved in 20 moves or less. Worldwide launch: 1980, Ideal Toy Company. Back In The Day: Lots of 90s kids found their parents' old Rubik's Cube from the 80s in a closet. Never solved it for real. Peeled the stickers off and put them back once, and showed everybody. Nobody believed it. They were right not to. Possible positions: About 43 quintillion. Word On The Playground: Took it apart with a screwdriver. Couldn't get it back together. One kid at school could solve it in a minute and everybody treated him like a wizard. Got one side done once. Took a picture. Never touched it again. 'God's number': 20 moves (proven 2010)
vhs-stack: The big VHS tower. VHS tapes, 1993, 1999. Childhood Pro Tip: Hold Play while you fast-forward to watch the previews zip by. It's also how VCRs get tired. Power Rangers premiere: August 28, 1993, Fox Kids. The Real Story: Power Rangers started on TV in 1993, built from Japanese fight scenes with American kids added in. The Pokémon cartoon came to the US in 1998 and the first movie in 1999. Tapes like these got watched until the boxes wore white. Power Rangers source: Japanese Super Sentai footage. Back In The Day: Every kid had a stack like this. Saturday morning shows, a few Disney movies and the tape you watched every day after school. These have been watched so many times the box art is worn white at the corners. The Pokémon tape has the Pikachu Thunderbolt part worn out. Pokémon anime (US): September 1998. Word On The Playground: Be kind, rewind. Power Rangers on the tape, a little rental sticker on the spine. Pokémon: The First Movie (US): November 1999.
vhs-loose: Loose tapes. VHS tapes, 1980s, 90s. Childhood Pro Tip: Want to save a tape forever? Snap out the little tab on the back. Then hide it from whoever owns the Scotch tape. Record-protect tab: A breakable tab on the back of the cassette. The Real Story: Every VHS tape has a little plastic tab on the back. Break it off and the VCR won't record over that tape. Put a piece of tape over the hole and it will, which is how 'DO NOT TAPE OVER' tapes got taped over. Tab removed: VCR refuses to record. Back In The Day: Tapes out of their cases, because the cases were in the other room, because nobody puts things back. In the 90s, every TV stand had a pile like this. One is labeled "DO NOT TAPE OVER" and has been taped over. Undo it: Cover the hole with tape. Word On The Playground: The cases are somewhere. Probably. Cases: Somewhere. Probably.
books: The book stack. Books, 1997, 2007. Childhood Pro Tip: Book report trick: read the first chapter, the last chapter and the back cover. Then the middle. Teachers ask about the middle. Harry Potter (US): September 1, 1998. The Real Story: Harry Potter came to the US in September 1998 and turned millions of kids into readers. Captain Underpants started in 1997. Diary of a Wimpy Kid didn't come out until 2007, so that one belongs to a little brother. Harry Potter (UK): June 26, 1997. Back In The Day: In the late 90s Harry Potter got kids reading books thicker than their arms. Kids read them at recess, at dinner and in the car, and a few years later whole towns had midnight parties for the new book. Captain Underpants: 1997, by Dav Pilkey. Word On The Playground: Book reports written from the back cover only. Diary of a Wimpy Kid: 2007, by Jeff Kinney.
poster-pokemon: Pokémon poster. Poster, 1998. Childhood Pro Tip: Hang a poster with tape rolled into loops on the back, not across the corners. It stays up longer and doesn't rip. Japan debut: February 27, 1996. The Real Story: Pokémon started in Japan in 1996 as a Game Boy game. Pikachu, number 25, became the face of it all because of the cartoon. In the US, posters from game magazines were the easiest way to get Pokémon on your wall. Created by: Satoshi Tajiri, Game Freak. Back In The Day: Posters came folded up in the middle of magazines, and kids pulled them out the second they got home. This one has staple holes right through Pikachu's face. It's still the best poster in the room. Pikachu's number: #025. Word On The Playground: Taped up, fell down, taped up again with way more tape. US games: Pokémon Red and Blue, September 1998.
poster-mummy: The Mummy poster. Movie poster, 1999, Universal. Childhood Pro Tip: Never hang a scary movie poster facing your bed. It watches. It always watches. Released: May 7, 1999. The Real Story: The Mummy came out in 1999, starring Brendan Fraser, a big action adventure remake of a 1932 monster movie. It made over $400 million, and its flesh-eating scarab beetles ruined a lot of sleepovers. Director: Stephen Sommers. Back In The Day: The Mummy was the big movie of summer 1999, and kids who were too young went anyway. The scarab beetle scene. That's all there is to say. Nobody slept.
